Tay-Sachs is an autosomal recessive disorder. In such cases, the disease phenotype only manifests in individuals who are homozygous for the recessive allele (aa). Genetic drift is the change in allele frequencies due to random sampling. Its magnitude is inversely proportional to the effective population size ($N_e$): the variance in allele frequency per generation is approximately $p(1-p)/2N_e$.

20,000 years ago, human populations were smaller and more fragmented, leading to a smaller $N_e$ and a more pronounced effect of drift (e.g., founder effects, bottlenecks). Today, global connectivity and larger population sizes increase the effective population size. As $N_e$ increases, the stochastic fluctuations of allele frequencies decrease, making genetic drift a less dominant force in the human gene pool compared to the Paleolithic.

Option (J) correctly identifies this mechanism.

Answer: (J)
